```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

evomod2 simulates populations of diploid individuals whose multivariate
phenotypes evolve under drift and Gaussian selection. Every simulation has
the same three ingredients:

1. a **model**: genetic architecture, mutation, recombination and
   environmental noise;
2. a list of **selection regimes**;
3. a call to **`evolve()`**, which returns a population with statistics
   recorded along the way.

This vignette walks through each one with small, fast simulations. The
other vignettes compare genetic architectures (`vignette("architectures")`)
and reproduce the simulations of Melo & Marroig (2015)
(`vignette("melo-marroig-2015")`).

```{r}
library(evomod2)
```

## Models

A genetic architecture says how genomes map to genotypic values `x`. In the
**additive** architecture, each allele carries an effect vector with one value
per trait, and `x` is the sum of the effect vectors of all alleles. Mutation
adds a multivariate normal vector to an allele's effects.

```{r}
model <- evomod_model(
  architecture = additive(loci = 20, traits = 4),
  mutation = mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.1),  # cov: sd 0.1 per trait, uncorrelated
  env_sd = 0.8,                                  # phenotype z = x + Normal(0, 0.8^2)
  init_sd = 0.1                                  # starting allelic effects
)
model
```

Generations are discrete by default; `life_cycle = moran()` gives
overlapping generations, where each generation is `n` birth-death events
(see `?life_cycles`). Other architectures are `binary_b()`, the binary ontogenetic matrix of the
original evomod model (with `binary_b_mutation()`), and `multilinear()`,
pairwise multilinear epistasis (see `?architectures`). Loci recombine freely
unless the model has a genetic map (`?recombination`).

## Selection regimes

Fitness is Gaussian around an optimum `theta`, with covariance `omega` (larger
`omega` means weaker selection):

```{r}
omega <- diag(10, 4)
regimes <- list(
  drift(100),                                                  # no selection
  stabilizing(300, omega = omega),                             # fixed optimum
  directional(300, delta_theta = c(0.02, 0.02, 0, 0), omega = omega)  # moving optimum
)
```

`directional()` moves the optimum by `delta_theta` every generation; here
traits 1 and 2 are pushed up while traits 3 and 4 stay put. `fluctuating()`
makes the optimum jump up or down every few generations, for all traits
together, independently, or in blocks (as in do O & Whitlock 2023):

```{r}
fluctuating(5000, every = 10, step = 0.2, omega = 1, structure = list(1:2, 3:4))
```

## Running a simulation

```{r}
pop <- evolve(model, regimes, n = 300, record_every = 10, seed = 1)
pop
```

Statistics are recorded every `record_every` generations:

```{r}
head(trait_means(pop))
tail(variances(pop))
g_matrices(pop)[["700"]]
```

`plot()` shows mean genotypic values against the optimum, additive variances,
or a genetic correlation (grey lines mark the regime boundaries):

```{r}
plot(pop)
```

```{r}
plot(pop, "variances")
```

```{r}
plot(pop, "correlation", traits = c(1, 2))
```

## Continuing a population

`evolve()` also takes a population and continues it: same individuals,
generation count, optimum and records.

```{r}
pop <- evolve(pop, stabilizing(200, omega = omega))
pop
```

Runs are reproducible: random numbers come from R's generator, so the same
`seed` (or `set.seed()`) gives the same result, and continuing a population
in two steps gives the same result as running it in one.

## Genomes and G matrix statistics

The current genomes are available as an array (rows x alleles x individuals;
alleles `2l - 1` and `2l` are the two copies of locus `l`):

```{r}
dim(genomes(pop))
```

For architectures where genotypic values are sums of allele effects, G splits
into a genic part (expected without linkage disequilibrium) and a linkage
disequilibrium part:

```{r}
dec <- g_decomposition(pop)
round(dec$genic, 3)
round(dec$ld, 3)
```

Matrix statistics for modularity and evolvability:

```{r}
G <- dec$G
avg_corr(G, modules = list(1:2, 3:4))   # within- and between-module correlations
autonomy(G, c(1, 1, 0, 0))               # autonomy in the direction of module 1
mean_autonomy(G)                         # mean over random directions
eigen_variance(G)                        # proportion of variance per eigenvector
```

## Larger simulations

The examples in `system.file("examples", package = "evomod2")` run larger,
replicated experiments from the command line, one replicate per process, so
they can run in parallel:

```{r}
list.files(system.file("examples", package = "evomod2"))
```
